newsitem.title: CHINA: China faces health disaster from smoking -official.
newsitem.headline: China faces health disaster from smoking -official.

text.p: Smoking kills half a million people a year in China and the country's huge army of puffers is costing it billions of dollars in tobacco-related losses, a United Nations health official said on Thursday.
"The biggest preventable cause of death in China is smoking," said Dr Roderick Gee, representative for the U.N.'s World Health Organisation (WHO) in China.
More than 300 million Chinese smoked cigarettes and some 500,000 of those died each year from tobacco-related illnesses, Gee said in an interview.
The number of smokers was increasing by three million a year and smoking deaths would soar to an annual two million people by 2025, Gee said.
"Disaster is approaching," Gee said. "With the present rates of smoking in China, 50 million of today's children will die prematurely of tobacco-related diseases."
China, home to 1.2 billion people, is the world's biggest cigarette market, with sales of 1.6 trillion cigarettes a year.

Although tobacco taxes were China's biggest source of state revenue, accounting for 71 billion yuan ($8.55 billion) or more than 10 percent of total government income, health care and other costs related to smoking far outstripped that, he said.
China collected 41 billion yuan in cigarette taxes in 1993, but economic losses caused by smoking such as disease, loss of labour and death, totalled 65 billion yuan, WHO figures show.
China says those losses totalled 70 billion yuan in 1994.
"China is realising now that despite the money which comes in from tobacco sales, the costs of treating the illnesses associated with tobacco may not be worth it," Gee said.
"Cutting down on the rates of smoking in China will have a big impact on the cost of health care in the future," he said.

Beijing had launched anti-smoking campaigns in recent years, slapping restrictions on cigarette advertising and banning smoking in public places, but greater efforts were needed to ensure future generations never took up the habit, Gee said.
"If it's not done now, it's going to be an enormous health problem for China in the future," he said.
Western tobacco companies, squeezed by hostile anti-smoking activism back home, were increasingly eyeing Asian countries such as China as new markets for their goods, he said.
In China, where more than 60 percent of men smoked compared to less than 10 percent of women, foreign cigarette firms would seek to target females, he said.
"This is a very big threat that international companies that tend to advertise more agressively than the local Chinese tobacco monopoly will target young people and women," he said.

While Beijing was gradually becoming aware of the economic costs of smoking, it was also under great pressure to open its markets to foreign goods -- including cigarettes, which now face stiff import tariffs, Gee said.
"You get health authorities in the United States saying this is bad, and trade authorities in the Unites States saying China must accept our cigarettes," Gee said.
